title: Simple Inventory
story: You've been hired to code the inventory system for a small shop. Apples, bananas, and milk come in and out every day. The shop owner needs to know: 'Do we have enough bananas for today's orders?' Time to build an inventory tracker!
why: Maps model real-world inventories perfectly — each item name maps to a quantity, and you can add stock, remove stock, and check availability with simple lookups.
analogy: An inventory Map is like a warehouse shelf label — each item has a card showing the current count. When stock arrives, you add to the number. When it leaves, you subtract. The card always shows what's actually there.
try_it: Add a `low_stock_alert` function that prints a warning when any item drops below 10 units. Then add a `restock_all` function that adds 50 to every item. For a challenge, track item prices in a second Map and compute total inventory value (quantity * price for each item summed together).
tips: When modifying a Map, use `&mut` to allow changes — without it, the function can only read
Default missing items to 0 — `match .get(&key) { Some(c) => c, None => 0 }` handles new items
Keepp functions focused: `add_stock` adds, `remove_stock` handles validation — don't mix concerns
common_mistakes: Using `=` instead of `.insert()` — `inv["apples"] = 50` doesn't work; use `inv.insert("apples", 50)`
Forgetting to re-insert after computing the new value — `.insert()` replaces the old value
Not handling `None` from `.get()` — new items won't be in the Map, so `None` means quantity 0
